claims.claim: A scope is the textual region of a program where a namespace is directly accessible, meaning an unqualified reference to a name looks the name up in that namespace.
If a name is bound in a block it is a local variable of that block unless declared global or nonlocal; a name bound at module level is a global variable.

At runtime Python searches three or four nested scopes in order: the innermost (local) scope first, then any enclosing function scopes, then the current module's global scope, and finally the built-in namespace (the LEGB order).
A variable created inside a function is local: it only exists inside the function and cannot be referenced from outside it (referencing it outside raises NameError).

By default, if no global or nonlocal statement is in effect, an assignment to a name goes into the innermost (local) scope; a local binding of an existing outer name shadows the outer one for the rest of that block.
The global statement makes named variables refer to and rebind bindings in the module's top-level namespace; nonlocal makes them refer to and rebind bindings in the nearest enclosing function scope.
A namespace is a mapping from names to objects; scope is the region where such a namespace is directly accessible, so namespace and scope are related but distinct ideas.

If a name-binding operation occurs anywhere in a block, all uses of that name in the block are treated as references to the local binding, which is why a name assigned later in a function is local for the whole function.

The worked example (a local y not visible outside show(); a local x in shadow() that shadows the global x without changing it; and a global-declared rebinding in change()) produces: y triggers NameError outside the function, the global x stays 'global' after shadow(), and becomes 'changed global' after change().
